evidence_cards.title: MEPS 2016: people with a reported ICD-10 A69 (other spirochetal infections, which includes Lyme disease)
evidence_cards.definition: People with at least one condition record whose 3-character ICD10CDX equals A69.
evidence_cards.method: Sum of unique-person weights (PERWT16F) over the domain; standard error by Taylor linearisation over VARSTR/VARPSU. Person-level, one year only.
comparability: A69 is the broad category that contains Lyme (A69.2x); MEPS public files keep only the first 3 characters, so this is NOT a Lyme-specific count and must not be read as Lyme prevalence.
MEPS panels overlap across adjacent years: never add or pool these yearly totals.
Condition rows come from household reports coded by professional coders.

AHRQ (MEPS team, 2026-09-24) urges caution forming Lyme cost estimates from MEPS: pooling 2016-2024 gives only about 300-400 observations, expenditures are highly skewed (about 1,000 or more are needed for a solid mean), only treated Lyme is identified (zero-expenditure cases drop out, biasing upward), events may be flagged as arthritis without naming Lyme, comorbidities cannot be separated from Lyme, and onset dates are not recorded. Lyme-specific A69.2 is available only in restricted data centers.

uncertainty.note: Small samples give very wide, unreliable intervals.

evidence_cards.summary: 2016: about 436,208 people (95% CI 250,739 to 621,678; 31 sampled persons) reported a condition coded A69.
evidence_cards.how_to_use: Cross-check or population context only, never a prevalence of Lyme or Long COVID; not a cost estimate (events are counts, not dollars).

contextual_issues: Caregiving burden: the questionnaire asked whether someone helped with housework or looked after the patient/family due to LD, and whether that help was paid, but the study explicitly did not ask patients to estimate unpaid time lost from household production, so unpaid caregiver time is mentioned but not quantified.
Lyme vaccine (LYMErix)-related costs were collected via the questionnaire (Appendix 1, section 6) but patients who received the vaccine were excluded from this study's reported cost results.
Insurance coverage status was asked in the questionnaire (yes/no for office visit and vaccination costs) but is not reported as a quantified outcome in the article's results.
Intangible costs such as pain and suffering were explicitly excluded from the cost estimate.
Public health surveillance and administration costs were explicitly not incorporated into the cost estimate.

The document cites another study (Steer et al.) reporting that approximately 7% of LD cases remained asymptomatic within a 20-month study, and notes these asymptomatic patients may have costs beyond this study's window, but this percentage is from a different cited study, not measured by this study itself.
Costs incurred by a patient beyond the 4-year (1997-2000) study period, including from long-term or chronic sequelae, were explicitly noted as omitted.

Maryland's overall Lyme disease incidence is noted as more than twice the US overall incidence (13.0 vs 6.3 cases per 100,000 population), used to justify choosing this endemic region for the study, but this is an incidence-rate comparison, not a cost figure.
evidence_gaps: Longitudinal cost data extending beyond the 4-year (1997-2000) study window would be needed to capture costs of long-term or chronic Lyme disease sequelae.

A nationally or multi-regionally representative sample would be needed, since all cost data come from only 5 Maryland Eastern Shore counties and may not generalize to other endemic or non-endemic regions.

Indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss costs were collected via questionnaire only in 1997-1998, from an overall survey response rate of approximately 22% and representing only about 8% of the total 3,415-patient study population; a larger, more representative response would allow more precise and less extrapolation-dependent estimates.

A reconciliation between the clinical case definition used to identify patients in this study and the CDC surveillance case definition used for the national 23,763-case count would be needed before combining the two into a single nationwide cost estimate.
Updated price-year data would be needed, since all cost figures in this study are expressed in year-2000 (or, for the national extrapolation, labeled 2002) dollars and are now nearly two decades old.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the Maryland Eastern Shore clinical case definition (physician determination from medical records, 5 counties, 1997-2000) with the national CDC surveillance case definition (physician-diagnosed EM>5cm or late manifestation plus laboratory evidence, nationwide, 2002) - the document itself states its clinical definition 'may have overestimated the number of LD cases' relative to the surveillance definition, while separately stating the surveillance-based national count is 'believed to be underreported' - these are two distinct, independently-stated and oppositely-directioned caveats about different parts of the extrapolation chain and must not be conflated into one combined 'true number' claim.

Do not treat mean and median per-patient cost figures as interchangeable: the document explicitly states a 'large difference ... between mean and median values, with the latter often less than half of the mean value,' and warns that using the mean to estimate national impact 'could be an overestimation.'

The ≈$203 million nationwide estimate combines a per-patient cost figure derived from data expressed in year-2000 dollars ($2,970 + $5,202) with a 2002 national case count, and the document itself labels the resulting total 'in 2002 dollars' without re-adjusting the per-patient cost component to 2002 price levels - this price-year mismatch within the document's own calculation should not be smoothed over in a simulator.

Direct medical costs were collected via medical record abstraction for all four study years (1997-2000), while indirect medical costs, nonmedical costs, and productivity losses were collected only via patient questionnaire restricted to 1997-1998 - these two cost-category groups do not share the same measurement time window and should not be presented as directly comparable year-by-year series.

The $2,970 (direct) + $5,202 (indirect/nonmedical/productivity) per-patient figures used in the nationwide extrapolation apply only to the subset of patients with clinically defined early- or late-stage LD (490 and 84 cases respectively), not to the full study population, which also includes suspected LD, tick bite, and other related complaints groups with much lower median costs ($108-$256) - do not apply the $2,970/$5,202 figures to the entire LD-relevant patient population.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Using multivariate linear regression analysis of direct medical costs, the study reports: 'No cost difference was seen between men and women.'

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The study's entire patient cohort (3,415 LD-relevant patients, from which all direct medical, indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss cost figures are derived) was identified through 'a final diagnosis code in their medical records' via medical record abstraction from health-plan and office-based provider charts, i.e., a diagnosis-code/chart-based ascertainment method rather than prospective symptom-based surveillance; patients without a qualifying diagnosis code, or without access to the healthcare encounter that would generate one, would not be captured in this cohort or its cost estimates.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The expected mean ($1,965) and median ($281) total cost per LD patient aggregated across all diagnosis groups, and the derived nationwide ≈$203 million estimate, are presented as single pooled figures with no breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status; sex was checked only for direct medical costs specifically (via regression, finding no difference), not for these pooled total-cost or nationwide figures.

decision_relevance.summary: This document is a societal-perspective cost-of-illness study of Lyme disease among patients in five Maryland counties (1997-2000), combining medical-record direct medical cost data with patient-reported indirect, nonmedical, and productivity-loss costs, and extrapolating to a rough nationwide estimate. A simulator built on it could let patients/advocates see how historical US Lyme disease costs differed by disease stage, let care delivery teams compare direct-medical-cost components (visits, serology, therapy, hospitalization) by diagnosis stage and study year, and let payers/policy audiences explore how stage-of-diagnosis and case-definition choices affect per-patient and population-level cost estimates. Because the data are nearly two decades old, drawn from a single endemic region, and mix at least two different price years in the national extrapolation, any simulator should present these as historical reference points rather than current cost benchmarks.
use_cases: Patients/advocates could explore how per-patient total costs differed between early-stage (median $397) and late-stage (median $923) Lyme disease in this 1997-2000 Maryland cohort, illustrating the potential value of earlier diagnosis, while being shown these are historical, single-region, year-2000-dollar figures rather than current national costs.

Payers/policy users could examine the $2,970 direct-medical-cost-per-patient and $5,202 indirect/nonmedical/productivity-cost-per-patient figures alongside the document's own flagged price-year and case-definition mismatches in the ≈$203 million nationwide extrapolation, to understand the limits of scaling a single-region cost study to a national policy estimate.

contextual_issues: Caregiving burden: the questionnaire asked whether someone helped with housework or looked after the patient/family due to LD, and whether that help was paid, but the study explicitly did not ask patients to estimate unpaid time lost from household production, so unpaid caregiver time is mentioned but not quantified.
Lyme vaccine (LYMErix)-related costs were collected via the questionnaire (Appendix 1, section 6) but patients who received the vaccine were excluded from this study's reported cost results.
Insurance coverage status was asked in the questionnaire (yes/no for office visit and vaccination costs) but is not reported as a quantified outcome in the article's results.
Intangible costs such as pain and suffering were explicitly excluded from the cost estimate.
Public health surveillance and administration costs were explicitly not incorporated into the cost estimate.

The document cites another study (Steer et al.) reporting that approximately 7% of LD cases remained asymptomatic within a 20-month study, and notes these asymptomatic patients may have costs beyond this study's window, but this percentage is from a different cited study, not measured by this study itself.
Costs incurred by a patient beyond the 4-year (1997-2000) study period, including from long-term or chronic sequelae, were explicitly noted as omitted.

Maryland's overall Lyme disease incidence is noted as more than twice the US overall incidence (13.0 vs 6.3 cases per 100,000 population), used to justify choosing this endemic region for the study, but this is an incidence-rate comparison, not a cost figure.
evidence_gaps: Longitudinal cost data extending beyond the 4-year (1997-2000) study window would be needed to capture costs of long-term or chronic Lyme disease sequelae.

A nationally or multi-regionally representative sample would be needed, since all cost data come from only 5 Maryland Eastern Shore counties and may not generalize to other endemic or non-endemic regions.

Indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss costs were collected via questionnaire only in 1997-1998, from an overall survey response rate of approximately 22% and representing only about 8% of the total 3,415-patient study population; a larger, more representative response would allow more precise and less extrapolation-dependent estimates.

A reconciliation between the clinical case definition used to identify patients in this study and the CDC surveillance case definition used for the national 23,763-case count would be needed before combining the two into a single nationwide cost estimate.
Updated price-year data would be needed, since all cost figures in this study are expressed in year-2000 (or, for the national extrapolation, labeled 2002) dollars and are now nearly two decades old.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the Maryland Eastern Shore clinical case definition (physician determination from medical records, 5 counties, 1997-2000) with the national CDC surveillance case definition (physician-diagnosed EM>5cm or late manifestation plus laboratory evidence, nationwide, 2002) - the document itself states its clinical definition 'may have overestimated the number of LD cases' relative to the surveillance definition, while separately stating the surveillance-based national count is 'believed to be underreported' - these are two distinct, independently-stated and oppositely-directioned caveats about different parts of the extrapolation chain and must not be conflated into one combined 'true number' claim.

Do not treat mean and median per-patient cost figures as interchangeable: the document explicitly states a 'large difference ... between mean and median values, with the latter often less than half of the mean value,' and warns that using the mean to estimate national impact 'could be an overestimation.'

The ≈$203 million nationwide estimate combines a per-patient cost figure derived from data expressed in year-2000 dollars ($2,970 + $5,202) with a 2002 national case count, and the document itself labels the resulting total 'in 2002 dollars' without re-adjusting the per-patient cost component to 2002 price levels - this price-year mismatch within the document's own calculation should not be smoothed over in a simulator.

Direct medical costs were collected via medical record abstraction for all four study years (1997-2000), while indirect medical costs, nonmedical costs, and productivity losses were collected only via patient questionnaire restricted to 1997-1998 - these two cost-category groups do not share the same measurement time window and should not be presented as directly comparable year-by-year series.

The $2,970 (direct) + $5,202 (indirect/nonmedical/productivity) per-patient figures used in the nationwide extrapolation apply only to the subset of patients with clinically defined early- or late-stage LD (490 and 84 cases respectively), not to the full study population, which also includes suspected LD, tick bite, and other related complaints groups with much lower median costs ($108-$256) - do not apply the $2,970/$5,202 figures to the entire LD-relevant patient population.

sex_gender_findings.finding: Using multivariate linear regression analysis of direct medical costs, the study reports: 'No cost difference was seen between men and women.'

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: The study's entire patient cohort (3,415 LD-relevant patients, from which all direct medical, indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss cost figures are derived) was identified through 'a final diagnosis code in their medical records' via medical record abstraction from health-plan and office-based provider charts, i.e., a diagnosis-code/chart-based ascertainment method rather than prospective symptom-based surveillance; patients without a qualifying diagnosis code, or without access to the healthcare encounter that would generate one, would not be captured in this cohort or its cost estimates.

subgroup_disaggregation_caveat.pooled_value: The expected mean ($1,965) and median ($281) total cost per LD patient aggregated across all diagnosis groups, and the derived nationwide ≈$203 million estimate, are presented as single pooled figures with no breakdown by age, race/ethnicity, disability status, sexual orientation, gender identity, veteran status, or marital/familial status; sex was checked only for direct medical costs specifically (via regression, finding no difference), not for these pooled total-cost or nationwide figures.

decision_relevance.summary: This document is a societal-perspective cost-of-illness study of Lyme disease among patients in five Maryland counties (1997-2000), combining medical-record direct medical cost data with patient-reported indirect, nonmedical, and productivity-loss costs, and extrapolating to a rough nationwide estimate. A simulator built on it could let patients/advocates see how historical US Lyme disease costs differed by disease stage, let care delivery teams compare direct-medical-cost components (visits, serology, therapy, hospitalization) by diagnosis stage and study year, and let payers/policy audiences explore how stage-of-diagnosis and case-definition choices affect per-patient and population-level cost estimates. Because the data are nearly two decades old, drawn from a single endemic region, and mix at least two different price years in the national extrapolation, any simulator should present these as historical reference points rather than current cost benchmarks.
use_cases: Patients/advocates could explore how per-patient total costs differed between early-stage (median $397) and late-stage (median $923) Lyme disease in this 1997-2000 Maryland cohort, illustrating the potential value of earlier diagnosis, while being shown these are historical, single-region, year-2000-dollar figures rather than current national costs.

Payers/policy users could examine the $2,970 direct-medical-cost-per-patient and $5,202 indirect/nonmedical/productivity-cost-per-patient figures alongside the document's own flagged price-year and case-definition mismatches in the ≈$203 million nationwide extrapolation, to understand the limits of scaling a single-region cost study to a national policy estimate.

spec.title: Lyme Disease Economic Burden Simulator (Maryland Eastern Shore, 1997-2000)
spec.boundary: This simulator models a 2006 CDC-authored peer-reviewed cost-of-illness study of Lyme disease among patients in five Maryland Eastern Shore counties, 1997-2000, covering per-patient direct medical, indirect medical (extra drug costs), nonmedical (paid help, travel), and productivity-loss costs by disease stage, plus the study's own extrapolation to a nationwide total using a 2002 national case count. It does not model costs beyond the 4-year study window, costs from other regions, intangible costs such as pain and suffering, public health administration costs, unpaid caregiver time (the study asked about this but did not quantify it), vaccine-related costs, or any demographic disaggregation beyond the single sex comparison the study reports.

takeaway.patient: This historical study of Lyme disease patients in five Maryland counties (1997-2000) found that the typical ('median') total cost - combining medical bills, extra out-of-pocket drug costs, paid help or travel, and lost work time - was higher for patients diagnosed with late-stage Lyme disease than for those diagnosed at an early stage, with late-stage typical cost running a little more than twice the early-stage typical cost in this cohort. These are historical, year-2000-dollar figures from one US region, and the study only observed an association between diagnosis stage and cost - it did not test whether earlier diagnosis itself causes lower costs.
takeaway.care: In this 1997-2000 Maryland cohort, median and mean total costs were substantially higher for late-stage than early-stage clinically diagnosed Lyme disease patients, and mean therapy and hospitalization/ER cost components both declined between 1997 and 2000. The indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss cost data came only from a 1997-1998 questionnaire subsample, a narrower window than the 1997-2000 direct-medical-cost data, so these cost categories should not be read as a single consistent time series. The study also used a clinical (chart-based) case definition distinct from the CDC surveillance case definition used nationally.
takeaway.policy: The study's own nationwide extrapolation, combining a per-patient cost figure from clinically defined early/late-stage Maryland patients with the 23,763 Lyme disease cases reported to CDC nationally in 2002, produced a stated headline estimate of about $203 million. Recomputing this directly from the document's own reported per-patient components and national case count instead yields about $194 million - a gap the document does not explain. The document also labels its total '2002 dollars' without adjusting the underlying year-2000-dollar per-patient costs, and separately cautions that its clinical case definition may have overestimated cases relative to the CDC surveillance definition used for the national count, while the surveillance-based count itself is believed to undercount true disease occurrence - two distinct, unresolved caveats.

patient: When discussing a Lyme disease diagnosis with a clinician, consider asking whether it is being treated as early-stage or late-stage, since this 1997-2000 Maryland study found typical costs differed by stage.
Keep in mind the study found an association between diagnosis stage and cost, not proof that catching Lyme disease earlier itself prevents higher costs later.
Treat these figures only as a rough historical reference point from one US region in year-2000 dollars, not as an estimate of what Lyme disease might cost someone today.
If facing out-of-pocket drug costs, travel expenses, or paid help related to Lyme disease, consider keeping your own records, since the study found these costs varied widely by stage of diagnosis.
care: This study's finding that late-stage patients had substantially higher typical and mean costs than early-stage patients may be worth checking against your own intake and staging documentation to see how stage classification at diagnosis relates to anticipated resource needs.

Because the indirect-cost and productivity-loss data came only from a 1997-1998 questionnaire subsample rather than the full 1997-2000 period used for direct medical costs, any local benchmarking effort would need its own data collection spanning comparable years.

Since the study used a clinical case definition different from the CDC surveillance case definition used nationally, teams comparing local caseloads to national case counts may want to clarify which definition any benchmark is using.

The documented decline in mean therapy and hospitalization/ER cost components between 1997 and 2000 may be worth examining against your own cohort's data as a possible indicator of care-pattern shifts over time, keeping in mind this reference is now roughly two decades old.
policy: Before using either the document's stated ~$203 million figure or the ~$194 million recomputation from its own components for budgeting, confirm which case definition and price-year assumptions apply, since the document itself flags both a case-definition mismatch (clinical vs. CDC surveillance) and an unreconciled price-year label.

Consider whether updated, multi-regional Lyme disease cost data would better support current budget-impact estimates, since this figure is drawn entirely from one Maryland region's 1997-2000 experience.
When choosing between mean and median cost inputs for any budget-impact estimate, note the document's own warning that using mean rather than median values could overestimate nationwide impact.

Given that the underlying patient cohort was identified through medical-record diagnosis codes, consider that this estimate likely does not capture Lyme disease cases without a qualifying diagnosis code, which would understate true disease burden and cost.

inputs.source: p.654/p.658, citing CDC national surveillance count for 2002; 15000-35000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source

outputs.label: Late-stage minus early-stage median total cost (always positive here; higher = larger late-stage cost premium)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the study's reported late-stage and early-stage median total costs in this 1997-2000 Maryland cohort; the document reports late-stage costs higher in every cost measure it presents, and the input ranges above are set so this gap cannot be pushed negative, consistent with that finding. It reflects an association the study observed between diagnosis stage and typical cost, not evidence that earlier diagnosis itself prevented higher costs.

outputs.label: Late-stage to early-stage median cost ratio
outputs.interpretation: This divides the late-stage median total cost by the early-stage median total cost; at default values it computes to about 2.3, meaning a typical late-stage patient's total cost was a little more than twice a typical early-stage patient's total cost in this cohort. The document reports these as medians, not means, and separately notes its mean values are far higher, so the two should not be used interchangeably.

outputs.label: Combined per-patient cost used in nationwide extrapolation
outputs.interpretation: This adds the document's own per-patient direct medical cost figure to its per-patient indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss figure, both restricted to clinically defined early- or late-stage patients; at default values it reproduces the document's own $8,172 per-patient figure used as the basis for its nationwide extrapolation below.

outputs.label: Recomputed nationwide economic impact (combined per-patient cost x national case count)
outputs.interpretation: This multiplies the combined per-patient cost above by the national case count to recompute the nationwide estimate the document itself derived. At default values this computes to about $194 million, somewhat lower than the document's own stated headline figure of about $203 million; the document does not explain this gap, and it should not be assumed to be rounding. The document also labels its headline total '2002 dollars' while the per-patient cost components here are year-2000 dollars, a price-year mismatch the document itself does not reconcile, and separately cautions that the national case count uses a CDC surveillance case definition while the per-patient costs come from a different clinical case definition the document says may have overestimated cases relative to surveillance - two distinct, independently stated caveats that should not be merged into one single 'true number' claim.

scenarios.label: Costlier case mix (more late-stage)
scenarios.goal: Tests how much the pooled extrapolation cost rises if patients skewed more toward costlier late-stage disease.
scenarios.description: Sets both extrapolation cost inputs to their assumed higher bound to show the blended per-patient cost under a case mix weighted toward more costly late-stage cases than the observed 1997-2000 sample, illustrative only.

scenarios.label: Lower-cost case mix (more early-stage)
scenarios.goal: Tests how much the pooled extrapolation cost falls if patients skewed more toward less-costly early-stage disease.
scenarios.description: Sets both extrapolation cost inputs to their assumed lower bound to show the blended per-patient cost under a case mix weighted toward less costly early-stage cases, illustrative only.

scenarios.label: Higher national case count (believed undercount)
scenarios.goal: Tests how much larger the nationwide estimate becomes if the true case count exceeded the reported surveillance figure.
scenarios.description: Raises the national case count to an assumed higher value, consistent with the document's own statement that the CDC-reported surveillance count is believed to be underreported.

scenarios.label: Combined worst-case underestimate
scenarios.goal: Tests how large the nationwide total could be if both the cost mix and case count were understated, as the authors caution.
scenarios.description: Combines the higher-cost case-mix assumption with a higher assumed national case count to illustrate how much larger the nationwide estimate could be than the document's reported approximately $203 million, consistent with its own caution that the estimate is likely too low.

## Source
Zhang et al., "Economic Impact of Lyme Disease," Emerging Infectious Diseases (CDC), 2006. Costs are drawn from medical-record abstraction (direct medical costs, 1997-2000) and a mailed patient questionnaire (indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss costs, 1997-1998 only) for Lyme disease patients in five Maryland Eastern Shore counties.

## What the numbers measure
Median and mean total costs are reported separately by diagnosis stage (early vs. late, clinically defined from medical records) and by other groups (suspected Lyme disease, tick bite only, other complaints). The document explicitly warns that mean values are often more than double the median for this cost data, so using means for extrapolation could overestimate impact. A per-patient direct medical cost ($2,970) and a per-patient indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss cost ($5,202), both restricted to the 490/84 clinically defined early- or late-stage cases respectively, were multiplied by the 23,763 Lyme disease cases reported to CDC nationally in 2002 to produce a stated ~$203 million nationwide estimate.

## Limitations stated in or implied by the document
The patient cohort (3,415 people) was identified through diagnosis codes in medical records rather than prospective surveillance; patients without a qualifying coded encounter would not appear in these cost estimates, so the figures likely undercount the true number and cost of Lyme disease cases. The pooled total-cost figures (median $281, mean $1,965) and the nationwide estimate have not been broken down by age, race/ethnicity, or other demographics; the document checked sex only for direct medical costs specifically, finding no difference, not for these pooled or nationwide figures. Federal survey sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support this kind of disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it. The document's own clinical case definition and the CDC's national surveillance case definition are different and are explicitly flagged by the authors as pulling in opposite directions (the clinical definition may have overestimated cases; the surveillance definition is believed to undercount them), so the two should not be combined into a single 'true' burden claim. Indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss costs were collected only in 1997-1998 from an approximately 22% questionnaire response rate (about 8% of the full cohort), a narrower and less representative window than the 1997-2000 direct medical cost data. Costs beyond the 4-year study period, intangible costs (pain and suffering), public health administration costs, and unpaid caregiver time are explicitly excluded from this estimate.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

- Expected mean total cost per LD patient, aggregated across all diagnosis groups: 1,965.00 in 2000 dollars is about 3,673.74 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.870). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Expected median total cost per LD patient, aggregated across all diagnosis groups: 281.00 in 2000 dollars is about 525.35 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.870). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Extrapolated nationwide annual economic impact of LD and relevant complaints: 203,000,000 in 2002 dollars is about 363,281,984 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.790). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Per-patient direct medical cost (clinically defined early or late stage), used in nationwide extrapolation: 2,970.00 in 2000 dollars is about 5,552.68 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.870). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Per-patient indirect medical + nonmedical + productivity-loss cost (clinically defined early or late stage), used in nationwide extrapolation: 5,202.00 in 2000 dollars is about 9,725.60 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.870). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Mean direct medical cost, clinically defined early-stage LD, 1997 cohort: 1,609.00 in 2000 dollars is about 3,008.17 in 2025 dollars (CPI-U all items, x1.870). This is general price inflation, not medical-care inflation, and is a restatement, not a measurement. Federal source: published price index, 1913-2025; computed in code from the federal file; no AI model.
- Lyme disease cases reported to CDC nationally (2002, the United States): the document reports 23,763; CDC's reported cases were 23,763 (confirmed and probable together), so the document's figure is within 10% of the CDC confirmed-plus-probable total (+0.0% versus the total). Definitions may differ between the document and CDC surveillance, so a gap is a prompt to check, not an error. Because the indirect-cost and productivity-loss data came only from a 1997-1998 questionnaire subsample rather than the full 1997-2000 period used for direct medical costs, any local benchmarking effort would need its own data collection spanning comparable years.

Since the study used a clinical case definition different from the CDC surveillance case definition used nationally, teams comparing local caseloads to national case counts may want to clarify which definition any benchmark is using.

The documented decline in mean therapy and hospitalization/ER cost components between 1997 and 2000 may be worth examining against your own cohort's data as a possible indicator of care-pattern shifts over time, keeping in mind this reference is now roughly two decades old.
policy: Before using either the document's stated ~$203 million figure or the ~$194 million recomputation from its own components for budgeting, confirm which case definition and price-year assumptions apply, since the document itself flags both a case-definition mismatch (clinical vs. CDC surveillance) and an unreconciled price-year label.

Consider whether updated, multi-regional Lyme disease cost data would better support current budget-impact estimates, since this figure is drawn entirely from one Maryland region's 1997-2000 experience.
When choosing between mean and median cost inputs for any budget-impact estimate, note the document's own warning that using mean rather than median values could overestimate nationwide impact.

Given that the underlying patient cohort was identified through medical-record diagnosis codes, consider that this estimate likely does not capture Lyme disease cases without a qualifying diagnosis code, which would understate true disease burden and cost.

inputs.label: Early-stage median total cost
inputs.source: p.657, Results/Figure 3 and Abstract; 200-600 range is an assumed exploration bound around the reported $397 median, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported median total cost (direct medical + extra drug costs + nonmedical costs + lost work time) for patients clinically diagnosed with early-stage Lyme disease in this Maryland cohort; moving it changes the stage cost gap and ratio outputs below.

inputs.label: Late-stage median total cost
inputs.source: p.657, Results/Figure 3 and Abstract; 700-1200 range is an assumed exploration bound around the reported $923 median, chosen so it cannot fall below the early-stage input's range, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported median total cost for patients clinically diagnosed with late-stage Lyme disease in the same cohort; a higher value answers how much more a typical late-stage diagnosis cost than early-stage in this historical dataset.

inputs.label: Per-patient direct medical cost (extrapolation input)
inputs.source: p.658, Discussion ($1,455,081 total direct medical cost / 490 clinically defined early- or late-stage cases); 2000-4000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the per-patient direct medical cost the document itself used for its nationwide extrapolation, covering only the 490 patients with a clinically defined early- or late-stage diagnosis; raising or lowering it tests how sensitive the nationwide estimate below is to this one input.

inputs.label: Per-patient indirect, nonmedical, and productivity-loss cost (extrapolation input)
inputs.source: p.658, Discussion ($436,949 total indirect medical, nonmedical, and productivity-loss cost / 84 clinically defined early- or late-stage cases with questionnaire data); 3500-7000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the per-patient sum of extra drug costs, nonmedical costs, and lost-work-time costs the document used for its nationwide extrapolation, collected from an 84-patient questionnaire subsample surveyed in 1997-1998, a narrower window than the direct medical cost figure above; changing it tests the same sensitivity from the indirect/nonmedical/productivity side.

inputs.label: National Lyme disease cases reported to CDC
inputs.source: p.654/p.658, citing CDC national surveillance count for 2002; 15000-35000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source
inputs.interpretation: This is the number of Lyme disease cases reported to CDC nationally in 2002 under the surveillance case definition, which differs from the clinical case definition used to generate the per-patient cost inputs above; moving it explores how sensitive the nationwide total is to the national case count alone, holding per-patient costs fixed.

outputs.label: Late-stage minus early-stage median total cost (always positive here; higher = larger late-stage cost premium)
outputs.interpretation: This is the gap between the study's reported late-stage and early-stage median total costs in this 1997-2000 Maryland cohort; the document reports late-stage costs higher in every cost measure it presents, and the input ranges above are set so this gap cannot be pushed negative, consistent with that finding. It reflects an association the study observed between diagnosis stage and typical cost, not evidence that earlier diagnosis itself prevented higher costs.

outputs.label: Late-stage to early-stage median cost ratio
outputs.interpretation: This divides the late-stage median total cost by the early-stage median total cost; at default values it computes to about 2.3, meaning a typical late-stage patient's total cost was a little more than twice a typical early-stage patient's total cost in this cohort. The document reports these as medians, not means, and separately notes its mean values are far higher, so the two should not be used interchangeably.

outputs.label: Combined per-patient cost used in nationwide extrapolation
outputs.interpretation: This adds the document's own per-patient direct medical cost figure to its per-patient indirect/nonmedical/productivity-loss figure, both restricted to clinically defined early- or late-stage patients; at default values it reproduces the document's own $8,172 per-patient figure used as the basis for its nationwide extrapolation below.

outputs.label: Recomputed nationwide economic impact (combined per-patient cost x national case count)
outputs.interpretation: This multiplies the combined per-patient cost above by the national case count to recompute the nationwide estimate the document itself derived. At default values this computes to about $194 million, somewhat lower than the document's own stated headline figure of about $203 million; the document does not explain this gap, and it should not be assumed to be rounding. The document also labels its headline total '2002 dollars' while the per-patient cost components here are year-2000 dollars, a price-year mismatch the document itself does not reconcile, and separately cautions that the national case count uses a CDC surveillance case definition while the per-patient costs come from a different clinical case definition the document says may have overestimated cases relative to surveillance - two distinct, independently stated caveats that should not be merged into one single 'true number' claim.

scenarios.label: Costlier case mix (more late-stage)
scenarios.goal: Tests how much the pooled extrapolation cost rises if patients skewed more toward costlier late-stage disease.
scenarios.description: Sets both extrapolation cost inputs to their assumed higher bound to show the blended per-patient cost under a case mix weighted toward more costly late-stage cases than the observed 1997-2000 sample, illustrative only.

scenarios.label: Lower-cost case mix (more early-stage)
scenarios.goal: Tests how much the pooled extrapolation cost falls if patients skewed more toward less-costly early-stage disease.
scenarios.description: Sets both extrapolation cost inputs to their assumed lower bound to show the blended per-patient cost under a case mix weighted toward less costly early-stage cases, illustrative only.

scenarios.label: Higher national case count (believed undercount)
scenarios.goal: Tests how much larger the nationwide estimate becomes if the true case count exceeded the reported surveillance figure.
scenarios.description: Raises the national case count to an assumed higher value, consistent with the document's own statement that the CDC-reported surveillance count is believed to be underreported.

scenarios.label: Combined worst-case underestimate
scenarios.goal: Tests how large the nationwide total could be if both the cost mix and case count were understated, as the authors caution.
scenarios.description: Combines the higher-cost case-mix assumption with a higher assumed national case count to illustrate how much larger the nationwide estimate could be than the document's reported approximately $203 million, consistent with its own caution that the estimate is likely too low.
